issues.legal_issue: A civil court cannot entertain a suit seeking to determine whether property or an interest in it is evacuee property when that question is assigned to the statutory authorities.
material_facts: An administrative authority declared the house to be evacuee property after notice to the evacuee’s son, but without notice to the claimant.
The claimant later asserted that a will gave her ownership of the house, pursued proceedings before the statutory authorities, and then filed a civil suit seeking an injunction against eviction.
The suit asked the civil court to decide a claim of title bearing on whether the house was evacuee property.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not maintainable because the civil court’s jurisdiction to entertain or decide the question was barred.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4(1), 7, 8, 24, 27, 28 and 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, the statutory authorities determine whether property is evacuee property, with appeal and revision available and their orders given finality; section 46 bars civil and revenue courts from deciding that question, and section 4(1) gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent laws, including section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Ram Gopal Reddy v. Additional Custodian, approved S. M. Zaki v. The State of Bihar and Khalil Ahmad Khan v. Malka Meher Nigar Begum, and disapproved the relevant observation in Namazi v. Deputy Custodian Evacuee Property.

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_property_status: A claimant brought an ordinary civil suit seeking a determination of whether property or an interest in it had the relevant protected or excluded status.
predicates.statutory_process_assigns_property_class: A statutory administrative process assigns an authority the task of determining the property’s status after hearing interested persons.
predicates.statutory_review_and_finality_provided: The statutory process provides review by higher authorities and gives finality to their resulting orders.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges property status and a statutory process assigns that classification to an authority with review and finality, the civil court cannot adjudicate the property’s status.

issues.legal_issue: An authority charged with determining whether property is evacuee property may decide all relevant questions of fact and law, including complicated questions of title.
material_facts: The statutory authority had to determine whether the house belonged to an evacuee and was therefore evacuee property.
The claimant’s assertion that a will gave her ownership raised a question of title relevant to that determination.
The statutory scheme provided for appeal and revision from the initial decision.
issues.conclusion: The authority’s power to determine whether property is evacuee property includes deciding relevant questions of fact and law, whether simple or complicated.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act requires the Custodian to determine whether property is evacuee property; sections 24 and 27 provide appeal and revision. The Court held that this jurisdiction does not depend on a prior finding about a collateral fact and is not limited to simple factual questions. It relied on S. M. Zaki v. The State of Bihar and discussed Ram Gopal Reddy v. Additional Custodian.

predicates.administrative_property_classification_p: An administrative authority is conducting a proceeding assigned to it to determine whether property has a specified statutory status.
predicates.title_question_relevant: A question about ownership or title is relevant to deciding the property’s statutory status.

issues.definition: In an administrative proceeding to classify property, when title is relevant to that classification, the authority may decide all relevant questions of fact and law.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory bar on civil and revenue court jurisdiction does not bar the High Court’s jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution.
material_facts: The case concerned a statutory scheme that barred civil and revenue courts from deciding specified property-status questions.
The Court distinguished the jurisdiction of civil courts from the jurisdiction conferred on the High Court by the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The statutory provisions do not bar the High Court from exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 28 and 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act cannot bar jurisdiction conferred on the High Court by Article 226 of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A person invokes the High Court’s constitutional writ jurisdiction in a proceeding concerning administrative action.
predicates.challenge_to_administrative_action: The proceeding challenges action taken by an authority under a statutory administrative scheme.

issues.definition: When a person invokes constitutional writ jurisdiction to challenge administrative action, that jurisdiction is not barred.
